title: Strategies to reduce low-value preoperative testing for low-risk ambulatory surgery: a rapid review
subtitle: Ten-week rapid review for the regional executive committee
statement: Three years after regional guidance advised against routine preoperative tests for healthy adults having low-risk ambulatory surgery, 61 percent of such patients in a spring snapshot still had at least one advised-against test. The executive committee needs to know, within ten weeks, which strategies reduce low-value testing, by how much and for how long, and whether reducing tests changes same-day cancellations or perioperative harm.
whoAffected: Healthy adults having low-risk ambulatory surgery in eight hospitals, the surgeons, anaesthetists and pre-anaesthesia clinic staff who order tests, and the laboratories and imaging departments that perform them.
whatHurts: Unneeded tests cost patients time and anxiety, lead to further investigations and delays, and use laboratory and imaging capacity that other patients need.
currentPractice: Tests are often ordered by default before any clinician sees the patient; the regional guidance is published but not built into ordering systems or feedback.
whyNow: The committee meets in December (action EC-2026-44) and wants an evidence-based choice of strategies before revising the guidance.
constraints: Ten weeks until the executive committee meeting in December. A librarian two days a week and two analysts one day a week each. English-language reports only. No budget for full-text purchase beyond the library's subscriptions.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients having low-risk surgery receive only the tests that could change their care, without more cancellations or harm.
summary: Problem framed as a rapid review of strategies to reduce low-value preoperative testing and their balancing effects.
